title: The Point and the Payroll: Milton to Chichi Jima to Langley to a Grave on the Brazos
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Milton, Massachusetts: the birth on Adams Street
stops.date_confidence: Date attested. Two atlas coordinates exist for this house: the research pool gives 42.2495, -71.0662 for 173 Adams Street, which is the Milton town centroid, while prescott_bush.journey.json pins the house itself at 42.262, -71.055. The father's pin is inherited so that the two births share one point; the divergence is recorded, not resolved.
stops.campa: The second son of Prescott Bush and Dorothy Walker is born in the house on Adams Street and named for his mother's father, George Herbert Walker of St. Louis and Wall Street. The father is a sales executive at a rubber company in South Braintree, and will be a director of the Union Banking Corporation, a partner at Brown Brothers Harriman, and a senator from Connecticut. The name comes down the mother's line, and so does the money, and so does the granite point in Maine his grandfather bought in 1902. The family will not stay in Massachusetts a full year.
suggested_refs: The Bush house at 173 Adams Street, Milton, Massachusetts, birthplace of the forty-first president

stops.name: Greenwich, Connecticut: the family seat
stops.date_confidence: The pool attests 1925 with no month or day; defaulted to 1 January. The geography lens labels this pin the family home on Grove Lane and then corrects itself: 41.0262, -73.6282 is the town centre, and 15 Grove Lane lies about 1.4 km north-northwest. The correction allows either moving the pin or dropping the street name; the street name is dropped, because this coordinate is also the Greenwich pin of prescott_bush.journey.json and keeping it makes the pin shared.
stops.campa: The family moves to Greenwich, a commuting town on Long Island Sound, where the father takes the morning train to Wall Street and moderates the Representative Town Meeting for seventeen years. The boy grows up here with four siblings, is schooled at Greenwich Country Day through the eighth grade, and is taken north every summer to Walker's Point at Kennebunkport. The house rules are the mother's: no bragging, no counting your own runs, no first person where a third will do. He keeps the habit into the presidency, where television reads it as a man with nothing to say about himself.
suggested_refs: The Bush house at 15 Grove Lane, Greenwich, Connecticut

stops.name: Phillips Academy, Andover: the captaincies and the enlistment
stops.date_confidence: The pool attests the Andover years as 1937 to 1942 without months; September 1937 is supplied for the entering term and is not itself attested. The coordinate is corrected from the Andover town centroid given in the pool, 42.6584, -71.1367, to the Phillips Academy campus. Enlistment on his eighteenth birthday, 12 June 1942, is attested; the pool's chronology lens wrongly folds it into the 1943 commissioning entry, and the two events are separated here.
stops.campa: At Andover he captains the baseball team and the soccer team and is elected president of the senior class, and the war closes on the country while he does it. Henry Stimson, Secretary of War and an old Andover man, tells the class of 1942 at commencement to go to college first. Bush is standing in that audience on his eighteenth birthday. He enlists in the Navy the same day, six months after Pearl Harbor, without the college his father's world takes for granted, and he will not see New Haven for three years.
suggested_refs: Phillips Academy commencement, 12 June 1942, Henry Stimson's address to the graduating class
sources: Naval History and Heritage Command, Bush biography file

stops.name: Greenwich, the Christmas dance
stops.date_confidence: The pool attests a Christmas dance at Greenwich in 1941 and no more: no venue, no day. December is inferred from the word Christmas. The coordinate is the Round Hill Club pin carried by prescott_bush.journey.json, where the father held club championships; the club is the venue named by popular biography and is tradition here, not attestation.
stops.campa: Home from Andover for the holidays in his last school year, he is introduced at a dance to Barbara Pierce, sixteen years old, from Rye across the state line, daughter of the president of the McCall Corporation. He asks a friend to name the tune being played because it is a waltz and he cannot waltz. They are engaged within eighteen months, while he is flying, and married within three years. The marriage runs seventy-three years, longer than that of any other American president, and she outlives the presidency by twenty-five.
suggested_refs: The Round Hill Club, Greenwich, traditional site of the 1941 Christmas dance

stops.name: Naval Air Station Corpus Christi: the wings
stops.date_confidence: Commissioning date attested. The pool's chronology lens conflates enlistment on 12 June 1942 with this commissioning under the single date 1943-06-09; its own correction separates them and the correction is followed. Chapel Hill and Wold-Chamberlain Field are attested by the geography lens for 1942 and 1942-1943 without days, and are narrated here rather than pinned.
stops.campa: From enlistment he goes to preflight school at Chapel Hill, then to primary training on Stearman biplanes at Wold-Chamberlain Field outside Minneapolis, then down to the Texas coast. At Corpus Christi he is commissioned an ensign in the Naval Reserve and designated a naval aviator three days before his nineteenth birthday, one of the youngest pilots in the Navy. He is assigned to torpedo bombers: the Grumman Avenger, a single-engine aircraft with a crew of three, of whom the pilot sits highest and forward and has the best chance of getting out.
suggested_refs: Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, Texas, where Bush received his wings on 9 June 1943
sources: Naval History and Heritage Command, Bush biography file

stops.name: USS San Jacinto: the station in the Pacific
stops.date_confidence: The pool gives May 1944 for the first combat mission and no day. The coordinate is not a place: the geography lens marks the carrier at 15, 150 and tags the entry [R] with the note that the ship had no single fixed position. The pin is inherited exactly. Carrier landings are given as 128 by the chronology lens and as 126 to 128 by its own correction; the lower figure is used.
stops.campa: He joins Torpedo Squadron 51 aboard the light carrier San Jacinto and flies his first combat mission in May against Wake Island, a fortified atoll the American advance has decided to bypass rather than take. Through the summer the squadron works the Marianas and the Philippine Sea. He is promoted lieutenant junior grade on the first of August. By the end of the war he will have flown fifty-eight combat missions, logged twelve hundred and twenty-eight hours, and put an aircraft down on a moving deck more than a hundred and twenty-six times.
suggested_refs: USS San Jacinto (CVL-30) and Air Group 51 in the central and western Pacific, 1944-1945
sources: Naval History and Heritage Command, Bush biography file

stops.name: Chichi Jima: the water off the island
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction between lenses, recorded and not adjudicated: the chronology lens gives September 1944 with no day, the geography lens gives 2 September 1944. The later date is used and the disagreement stands.
stops.campa: His Avenger is hit by antiaircraft fire on a run against the Japanese radio station on Chichi Jima, in the Bonin Islands. He holds the aircraft on the target, releases, turns out to sea burning, and bails out. His two crewmen are killed. He comes down alone in the water and is pulled aboard the submarine Finback after hours adrift, with Japanese boats putting out from the island behind him. He is twenty years old. The Navy gives him the Distinguished Flying Cross and the Air Medal three times over, and in November he returns to the San Jacinto and goes back to work.
suggested_refs: The rescue of Lieutenant Bush by USS Finback off Chichi Jima, September 1944
sources: Naval History and Heritage Command, Bush biography file

stops.name: First Presbyterian Church, Rye: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Release from active duty is dated 1945-09-02 by the chronology lens; that is the date of the Japanese surrender aboard USS Missouri, and the lens's own correction gives only September 1945 for the release. The narrative therefore says September without a day.
stops.campa: On leave from the Pacific he marries Barbara Pierce in her hometown church at Rye, six days into the last year of the war. He is twenty and she is nineteen. His squadron is being retrained for the invasion of the Japanese home islands when the surrender comes in September and releases him from active duty before the invasion is ordered. The Navy discharges him formally, as a lieutenant, ten years later. From this church the marriage will move to New Haven, Odessa, Midland, Houston, New York, Beijing, and the Naval Observatory, and she will run every house of it.
suggested_refs: First Presbyterian Church, Rye, New York, 6 January 1945

segments.name: New Haven and the Permian Basin

stops.name: Yale, Old Campus: two and a half years
stops.date_confidence: The pool attests the Yale years as 1945 to 1948 without months; November 1945 stands for the entering term and is not itself attested. Graduation in 1948 with a B.A. in economics is attested, as are the fraternity presidency, the baseball captaincy, and Phi Beta Kappa. Skull and Bones comes from the geography lens citing Yale archives.
stops.campa: He enters Yale on the accelerated postwar schedule, among classes crowded with veterans older than he is, and finishes a degree in economics in two and a half years. He plays first base and captains the team into the first two College World Series, takes Phi Beta Kappa, presides over Delta Kappa Epsilon, and is tapped for Skull and Bones, the senior society his father entered in 1916, in the windowless brownstone on High Street. Prescott Bush sits on the Yale Corporation while his son is an undergraduate here.
suggested_refs: The Skull and Bones tomb on High Street, New Haven, entered by Prescott Bush in 1916 and by his son in 1948

stops.name: New Haven, the first son
stops.date_confidence: The research pool attests only the year 1946 and the city. The exact date and the coordinate are inherited byte-identical from prescott_bush.journey.json, where the same birth is stopped from the grandfather's side.
stops.campa: A son is born in New Haven while the father is still an undergraduate, and is named George Walker Bush for the great-grandfather in St. Louis. The grandfather Prescott is a partner at Brown Brothers Harriman and two years from his first campaign for the Senate. The child will grow up in Midland among the derricks, will hold in turn both of the offices his father holds, and will send an army in 2003 against the adversary his father fought to a ceasefire in 1991 and left standing in Baghdad. Two more sons and two daughters follow.
suggested_refs: Grace-New Haven Hospital, birthplace of the forty-third president, 6 July 1946
sources: QUEUE.md entry for George W. Bush

stops.name: Odessa, the Dresser posting
stops.date_confidence: The pool attests 1948 with no month or day; defaulted to 1 January, though the move followed the summer graduation. That Prescott Bush sat on the Dresser Industries board is not in this pool and comes from prescott_bush.journey.json.
stops.campa: Six months out of Yale, with the family firms and the Wall Street doors open to him, he takes work as an equipment clerk for a subsidiary of Dresser Industries and drives west to Odessa in the Permian Basin. His father sits on the Dresser board. Within two years the company moves the young family through Ventura, Bakersfield, and Compton in California and back to Texas again. The roads out to the leases are caliche and the gas burns off at the wellheads. Nobody in Odessa has heard of Greenwich.
suggested_refs: Dresser Industries oil-tool operations at Odessa, Texas, 1948

stops.name: Compton, California: the birth of Robin
stops.date_confidence: Birth date attested. The pool's chronology lens places this birth in Texas; its own correction, citing Wikipedia on Pauline Robinson Bush, places it in Compton, California, during the Dresser posting, and the correction is followed. The coordinate is the centre of Compton; the pool gives no address.
stops.campa: A daughter is born during the California postings and named Pauline Robinson Bush for her mother's mother. The family calls her Robin. The Dresser circuit runs on, Ventura to Bakersfield to Compton and back to Texas, and by 1950 they are settled in Midland. She is three years old, in the spring of 1953, when she wakes tired and stays tired, and the blood work comes back leukemia. The Midland doctor tells her parents she has a few weeks and advises them to take her home and let her go. They take her to New York instead.
suggested_refs: Pauline Robinson Bush, born Compton, California, 20 December 1949
sources: Wikipedia: George H. W. Bush (with correction)

stops.name: Midland, the independent companies
stops.date_confidence: The pool attests 1951 for Bush-Overbey, 1953 for Zapata Petroleum and for the birth of John Ellis Bush, and 1954 for the presidency of Zapata Offshore, in every case with no month or day. Dates default to 1 January.
stops.campa: He goes into business for himself with his neighbor John Overbey, buying royalty interests across the Permian Basin, in a town filling up with young couples from the East doing precisely the same thing. In 1953 the partnership merges with the Liedtke brothers to become Zapata Petroleum and drills the Jameson field, where the wells come in one after another. In February of that year a second son is born and named John Ellis Bush. By 1954 he is president of the offshore arm, Zapata Offshore, and the drilling has moved out to sea.
suggested_refs: Zapata Petroleum Corporation and the Jameson field, Coke County, Texas, 1953

stops.name: Memorial Hospital, New York: the death of Robin
stops.date_confidence: Date and city attested by the correction to the chronology lens, which also corrects the birthplace. The coordinate is the Memorial Hospital pin inherited from prescott_bush.journey.json, where the grandfather dies in 1972; the pool names only New York City, so the building is atlas inheritance, not attestation. The seven-month duration of treatment is the traditional figure.
stops.campa: For seven months the parents take turns at the hospital in New York while the transfusions hold the leukemia and then lose it. Robin dies on the eleventh of October 1953, two months short of her fourth birthday. Her father is twenty-nine. She is buried at Putnam Cemetery in Greenwich, in the ground where Prescott and Dorothy Bush will be laid, and in the year 2000 she is moved a second time, to Texas, into the plot on the grounds of her father's presidential library, where her parents will come to lie on either side of her.
suggested_refs: Putnam Cemetery, Greenwich, first grave of Robin Bush, 1953 to 2000

stops.name: Houston, Zapata Offshore
stops.date_confidence: The pool attests 1959 with no month or day; defaulted to 1 January.
stops.campa: He separates the offshore arm from the parent company, takes Zapata Offshore for himself, and moves it and the family from Midland to Houston, where the contracts and the banks are. The rigs work the Gulf of Mexico and, before long, waters a good deal further off. In Houston he becomes a friend of a young lawyer named James Baker, who will manage his campaigns, run the Treasury under Reagan, and hold the State Department for him through the war against Iraq.
suggested_refs: Zapata Offshore Company, Houston, and its Gulf of Mexico drilling contracts

stops.name: Houston, chairman of the Harris County Republicans
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested; no day given, defaulted to the first. The 1964 Senate defeat is attested to 1964 and the Zapata stock sale to 1966; the chronology lens files them out of order and they are narrated here in calendar order.
stops.campa: He is elected chairman of the Harris County Republican Party, the first office of any kind he has held, in a state where the Republicans are a minority organization and Houston holds their largest concentration of them. In 1964 he runs for the United States Senate against the incumbent Ralph Yarborough and is beaten, fifty-six percent to forty-four. Two years later he sells the last of his Zapata stock for something near a million dollars, which is the money that lets him stop working for a living and stand for office instead.
suggested_refs: The Harris County Republican organization, Houston, 1963-1966

stops.name: United States Capitol: the Seventh District
stops.date_confidence: The pool attests election in 1966 with 57 percent and service from 1967 to 1971; 3 January 1967 is the opening of the Ninetieth Congress and is supplied here rather than attested by the pool.
stops.campa: He takes Texas's Seventh District with fifty-seven percent of the vote and is seated on the Ways and Means Committee as a freshman, which no freshman has been given since 1904. He is returned unopposed in 1968. In 1970 he gives up the safe seat to run for the Senate a second time and is beaten by Lloyd Bentsen, fifty-four percent to forty-six. He has now lost two Senate races in Texas and will hold every office he holds from here by appointment, until a national ticket puts his name back on a ballot in 1980.
suggested_refs: The House Ways and Means Committee, Ninetieth Congress, and its freshman from Texas

stops.name: United Nations Headquarters: Resolution 2758
stops.date_confidence: The pool attests service from 1971 to 1973 and the Resolution 2758 vote in 1971, in both cases without months; defaulted to 1 January.
stops.campa: Nixon sends the twice-beaten Senate candidate to the United Nations as ambassador, an office for which he has no diplomatic training whatever. Through the autumn he works the delegations to keep the Republic of China in its seat, while his own White House is separately arranging its opening to the mainland behind him. Resolution 2758 passes, the Republic of China is expelled, and the People's Republic is seated to applause on the floor. The men who take the chair answer to Mao Zedong. Three years from now Bush will be the senior American in their capital.
suggested_refs: UN General Assembly Resolution 2758, 25 October 1971

stops.name: Republican National Committee, 1625 Eye Street: the Watergate year
stops.date_confidence: The pool attests the chairmanship for 1973-1974 without months; defaulted to 1 January. The address is tagged [R] at source: the geography lens gives it from period press accounts and notes that the committee later relocated.
stops.campa: Nixon moves him to the chairmanship of the Republican National Committee in the winter the burglars come to trial. For eighteen months he travels the country defending the president to state parties, repeating denials he has been given and believes. When the tape of the twenty-third of June 1972 is released, he writes to the president that resignation is now in the best interest of the country. Nixon resigns the following day. Bush is asked what he would like next, and, passing over London and Paris, he asks for China.
suggested_refs: Republican National Committee headquarters, 1625 Eye Street NW, Washington, in the Watergate years

stops.name: Beijing, the Liaison Office
stops.date_confidence: The pool attests 1974-1975 without months; defaulted to 1 January. The coordinate is city-level: the geography lens states that the office's precise historical street address is not confirmed.
stops.campa: He is sent to Beijing as chief of the United States Liaison Office, the senior American official in a country with which his own has no embassy and no formal relations. He and Barbara ride bicycles through a city of bicycles, and are watched doing it. Mao Zedong is alive and still governing. Bush is recalled after fourteen months. He will come back to this city in February 1989 as president of the United States, three weeks into the term, and in June of that year the army will clear Tiananmen Square while he is deciding how much to say.
suggested_refs: The United States Liaison Office, Beijing, 1974-1975, before formal recognition

stops.name: Central Intelligence Agency, Langley: the director's year
stops.date_confidence: Appointment date attested; he leaves on 20 January 1977. The 1976 renewal of Noriega's asset status is flagged inside manuel_noriega.journey.json as tradition, not FOIA-confirmed, and is stated here as tradition. Operation Condor is carried in the exact form the chronology lens carries it: as a note that the source records active American support during his tenure.
stops.campa: Ford brings him home to run the Central Intelligence Agency in the year after the Church Committee published the assassination plots and the mail openings. The Agency now has to answer questions in public. He holds the office three hundred and fifty-six days. Manuel Noriega, on the payroll since 1971, is kept on it, and tradition holds that Bush himself signed the renewal, though no FOIA record confirms it. Operation Condor, the Southern Cone's shared machinery of disappearance under Augusto Pinochet and his neighbors, runs with American support while Bush sits in this building. William Casey will inherit both files.
suggested_refs: CIA headquarters, Langley, Virginia, under Director George Bush, 1976-1977

stops.name: Detroit, the convention and the second place
stops.date_confidence: The pool attests the Detroit convention and the running-mate selection to 1980 with no month or day; 16 July 1980 is the nomination night and is supplied here, not attested by the pool. Iowa and New Hampshire are attested but carry no coordinates in the pool, so they are narrated rather than pinned. That Casey helped broker this ticket is a claim william_casey.journey.json examined and dropped as unsupported; it is not repeated.
stops.campa: He runs for the nomination in his own right, wins the Iowa caucuses over Ronald Reagan by thirty-one and a half points to twenty-nine and four tenths, then loses New Hampshire badly in a quarrel over the format of a debate, and withdraws in late May when Reagan has the delegates. At the convention in Detroit, Reagan offers him second place and he takes it. In November the ticket carries fifty and seven tenths percent of the popular vote and four hundred and eighty-nine electoral votes of five hundred and thirty-eight. William Casey, who ran Reagan's campaign, goes to Langley.
suggested_refs: The 1980 Republican National Convention, Joe Louis Arena, Detroit

stops.name: United States Naval Observatory: the vice president's house
stops.date_confidence: The pool attests the vice presidency as 1981-1989 and the residence at the Naval Observatory, and names the response to the 1981 assassination attempt among the crisis-management duties. The tag [R] the chronology lens placed on the vice presidency itself is a fetch artifact, not an evidentiary grade, and is corrected to attested by the pool's own note.
stops.campa: The house on the Naval Observatory grounds is his address for eight years, the longest he lives anywhere as an adult. Sixty-nine days into the first term Reagan is shot outside a Washington hotel and the vice president is in the air over Texas, flying back to a government uncertain who is running it. He chairs the crisis-management task forces, the terrorism task force, the deregulation task force. He attends the funerals of foreign heads of state. In public he says nothing for eight years that is not the president's line.
suggested_refs: Number One Observatory Circle, official residence of the vice president, 1981-1989

stops.name: Old Executive Office Building: the desk next door
stops.date_confidence: Diary date attested by National Security Archive EBB 210, which prints the excerpt with the ellipsis shown. The stop rests on an inference the interlock lens tags [R]: oliver_north.journey.json places North's desk in this building from 1981 but does not itself state where Bush's office was. The Walsh report finding on what Bush knew was never fetched in this research pass and is therefore not asserted.
stops.campa: His own office in the Old Executive Office Building stands along the corridor from the desk where Oliver North runs the resupply of the Nicaraguan contras out of the proceeds of missiles sold to Iran. William Casey is at Langley. Adnan Khashoggi is the middleman on the arms. Robert McFarlane has flown to Tehran in May with a cake and an inscribed Bible. On the fourth and fifth of November, as a Beirut weekly breaks the story, the vice president dictates his diary. In public, for the next six years, he will say that he was out of the loop.
stops.quote: I'm one of the few people that know fully the details ...
stops.quote_source: George H. W. Bush diary, 4-5 November 1986, as excerpted in National Security Archive Electronic Briefing Book No. 210; the ellipsis is the Archive's own
suggested_refs: National Security Archive Electronic Briefing Book No. 210, on Bush and Iran-Contra

stops.name: Louisiana Superdome, New Orleans: the six words
stops.date_confidence: Date attested; the acceptance speech text verified against the American Presidency Project transcript. The pool corrects one famous line: the transcript reads I want a kinder and gentler nation, not a kinder, gentler nation, and no printing drops the conjunction.
stops.campa: He accepts the nomination in the Superdome and gives the country three sentences it will keep: a thousand points of light, the community organizations spread like stars across the nation; a kinder and gentler nation; and six words about taxes. The hall hears the last of them as a pledge and the country will hold him to it. He signs a tax increase twenty-six months later, and the six words are read back to him in the advertisements of the campaign that turns him out.
stops.quote: Read my lips: no new taxes.
stops.quote_source: Address Accepting the Presidential Nomination at the Republican National Convention, New Orleans, 18 August 1988; transcript, The American Presidency Project
suggested_refs: The 1988 Republican National Convention acceptance speech, Louisiana Superdome

stops.name: The White House: the inauguration
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Miller Center and Wikipedia; inaugural text verified against the Avalon Project transcript. The coordinate is the White House pin used by the geography lens for the presidency as a whole; the oath itself was administered at the Capitol.
stops.campa: He is sworn in as the forty-first president, thanks Ronald Reagan from the platform for the wonderful things he has done for America, and calls the day a meeting on democracy's front porch. Dan Quayle is sworn in as vice president. The Cold War has eleven months left to run and nobody standing on that platform knows it. Three weeks from now he is back in Beijing as head of state. Before the year is out he meets Mikhail Gorbachev off Malta in a gale and sends an army into Panama to arrest a man his own Agency once paid.
stops.quote: We meet on democracy's front porch, a good place to talk as neighbors and as friends.
stops.quote_source: Inaugural Address, 20 January 1989; transcript hosted by the Avalon Project, Yale Law School
suggested_refs: The Inaugural Address of 20 January 1989 and its thousand points of light
sources: Miller Center: George H. W. Bush

stops.name: Marsaxlokk Bay: the summit in the storm
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Wikipedia on the Malta Summit and by the Bush Presidential Library.
stops.campa: He meets Mikhail Gorbachev in Marsaxlokk Bay aboard the Soviet liner Maxim Gorky, the delegations crossing between ships in a gale that cancels half the schedule and gives the meeting its nickname. Nothing is signed. No communique is issued. The Berlin Wall has been open three weeks and the governments of Eastern Europe are falling one after another while the two men sit in a stateroom in a storm. The press files it that week as the end of the Cold War, and the historians keep the reading afterward. Eleven months ago he was a vice president who said nothing in public.
suggested_refs: The Malta Summit aboard the Maxim Gorky, 2-3 December 1989

stops.name: Panama City: Operation Just Cause
stops.date_confidence: Attested. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from manuel_noriega, william_casey, agha_hasan_abedi and arthur_ben, in whose files it is already a shared pin; the interlock lens names it as the coordinate a Bush file would most naturally inherit. Bush directs from Washington and does not travel to Panama during the fighting.
stops.campa: American forces go into Panama at forty-six minutes past midnight to depose Manuel Noriega, who has been on the Agency's payroll since 1971 and whose status, tradition holds, was renewed in 1976 by the man now ordering the invasion. William Casey inherited the same relationship as director. Noriega's accounts sit in the BCCI branch on Calle 50 that Agha Hasan Abedi built, and he does not surrender until the third of January. Three months before the landings, an American veterans' delegation with Arthur Ben among it walked Casco Viejo watching this come.
stops.quote: My fellow citizens, last night I ordered U.S. military forces to Panama. No President takes such action lightly. This morning I want to tell you what I did and why I did it.
stops.quote_source: Address to the Nation Announcing United States Military Action in Panama, 20 December 1989; transcript, The American Presidency Project
suggested_refs: Operation Just Cause, 20 December 1989, and the surrender of Manuel Noriega on 3 January 1990
sources: Miller Center: George H. W. Bush

stops.name: The White House: the Americans with Disabilities Act
stops.date_confidence: The pool attests the signing to 1990 and names the Immigration Act of 1990 and the Clean Air Act amendments in the same year; 26 July 1990 is the signing date and is supplied here rather than given by the pool.
stops.campa: He signs the Americans with Disabilities Act. It forbids discrimination against disabled Americans in employment, in public accommodation and in transport, and it obliges the country to rebuild its doorways, its buses and its sidewalks to admit them. The Clean Air Act amendments and the Immigration Act of 1990 are signed in the same year. Seven days after the signing on the South Lawn the Iraqi army crosses into Kuwait, and the two and a half years of the term that remain go to the Gulf.
suggested_refs: The signing of the Americans with Disabilities Act, South Lawn of the White House, 26 July 1990

stops.name: Camp David: this will not stand
stops.date_confidence: The quotes lens tags this line [R]: widely attributed to remarks to reporters on 5 August 1990 and frequently cited in secondary sources, but not fetched from a primary transcript in this research pass. The Camp David pin is attested by the geography lens for the Gulf War planning sessions without a date of its own.
stops.campa: Iraq takes Kuwait on the second of August, and he spends the weekend at the presidential retreat working the telephone, calling capitals one after another to build a coalition that will include Arab armies. On the fifth, back at the White House, he stops before the helicopter and tells the reporters that this will not stand. Nothing in the American position before that sentence had committed the country to reversing the annexation; everything after it does. Brent Scowcroft, who will write the book of this year with him, is beside him throughout.
stops.quote: This will not stand, this aggression against Kuwait.
stops.quote_source: Remarks to reporters, 5 August 1990, widely cited; the research pool tags this quotation [R], not fetched from a primary transcript
suggested_refs: Camp David, Catoctin Mountain Park, and the Gulf War planning sessions of August 1990

stops.name: The White House: the war address
stops.date_confidence: Attested; transcript verified against the Miller Center presidential speeches archive.
stops.campa: Two hours after allied aircraft cross into Iraqi and Kuwaiti airspace he tells the country from the Oval Office that the war has begun and that no ground forces are engaged. The air campaign runs for weeks before any army moves. This is the war he has spent five months assembling by telephone, with the United Nations behind it and Arab armies inside it, and it is the first American war since Vietnam with a stated object and a stated limit. The object is the liberation of Kuwait. The limit is the liberation of Kuwait.
stops.quote: Just 2 hours ago, allied air forces began an attack on military targets in Iraq and Kuwait. These attacks continue as I speak. Ground forces are not engaged.
stops.quote_source: Address to the Nation on the Invasion of Iraq, 16 January 1991; transcript, Miller Center presidential speeches archive
suggested_refs: The Oval Office address of 16 January 1991 opening Operation Desert Storm
sources: Miller Center: George H. W. Bush

stops.name: Kuwait City: the occupation ends
stops.date_confidence: Attested by Miller Center. The coordinate is the pool's Kuwait City value; saddam_hussein.journey.json pins the Seif Palace, seized on 2 August 1990, two hundred metres away at 29.3777, 47.9791. That the ceasefire permitted Iraqi helicopter flights, and what those helicopters then did, is carried from that file rather than from this pool.
stops.campa: The ground war lasts a hundred hours. On the twenty-seventh of February the Iraqi occupation of Kuwait is finished and he orders the shooting stopped. Saddam Hussein remains in Baghdad and in power. The ceasefire terms let his helicopters fly on the grounds that the roads are destroyed, and the risings in the Shia south and the Kurdish north are put down under them within a fortnight. The coalition's mandate ran to the liberation of Kuwait and no further. Twelve years later his elder son will send an army to Baghdad.

stops.name: The White House: Souter and Thomas
stops.date_confidence: The chronology lens files both appointments under a single 1990 date; its own correction separates them, and the correction is followed. stops.campa: He appoints two justices to the Supreme Court in successive years. David Souter is nominated in July of 1990 and confirmed that October. Clarence Thomas is nominated on the first of July 1991, confirmed by fifty-two votes against forty-eight on the fifteenth of October, and sworn in eight days after that. The first nomination falls in the year of the Americans with Disabilities Act and the second in the year of the victory parades. Souter sits nineteen years. Thomas is still sitting on the day Bush is buried in 2018.

stops.name: Astrodome, Houston: the renomination

In November he loses to Bill Clinton. He has negotiated the North American Free Trade Agreement, which is ratified after he has gone. Eighteen months before the vote, with the Cold War over and the Gulf War won, his approval stood at eighty-nine percent. The country turns him out at the first opportunity, thinking about its own wages.

stops.name: Baidoa: New Year's Eve with the troops
stops.date_confidence: Tagged [R] at source: the geography lens rests it on Wikipedia plus contemporaneous news accounts of December 1992 and January 1993, without a primary itinerary.
stops.campa: With three weeks left in the presidency he flies to Somalia to see the troops he has sent to open the famine roads, and spends the last night of the year in Baidoa among soldiers and relief workers, in a town with no working government of any kind. The operation is called Restore Hope, and it is the last one he orders. He hands the mission to Bill Clinton twenty days later. He came into Washington as a congressman in 1967 and goes out of it standing in a food line in the Bay region.
